title: Ashtpadi 1, salok: I bow to the Guru
hookLine: aad gure namah: I bow to the primal Guru, the Guru of the ages, the True Guru (Sukhmani 1)

lines: SERIOUS THINGS BEGIN WITH A BOW.
cards: Before a match, a wrestler in a Punjabi village touches the earth of the pit, then his forehead. A musician touches the strings before playing; a dancer bows to the floor.
Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib when they come into its presence. Each begins a serious thing by lowering the head a little, first. Sukhmani begins like that too.
Before a single teaching, before peace or Name or anything else, Guru Arjan bows. Four times.

teach.b: Here is the salok that opens Sukhmani. Aad gure namah. Jugaad gure namah.
Satgure namah. Sri gurdeve namah. Each line ends with namah, a word of homage: I bow, I salute.
So the salok is four bows, each to a slightly different face of the same Guru.

teach.h: THE PRIMAL GURU, THE GURU OF AGES.
teach.b: Aad gure: the Guru of the beginning, the primal Guru, there before anything began. Jugaad gure: the Guru through all the ages, jug being the great ages of time. Satgure: the True Guru.

teach.h: THE TRUE GURU, THE DIVINE GURU.
teach.b: And Sri gurdeve: the great, divine Guru, the Guru who shines. Who is this Guru? In the Sikh reading of this salok, the Guru is God, the One who teaches.
Sikhs also honor the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru's voice in the world, but here the bows go to the One beyond time.
Listen to how the salok moves: from the very beginning, across all ages, to what is true, to what shines. A bow that travels from the first moment to this one.

Some listeners hear an echo of Japji's opening salok, which praises the One true in the beginning and true through the ages; Guru Arjan sets Sukhmani in the same frame. And notice the order he chooses.
The jewel of peace doesn't begin with peace.
It begins with bowing. Peace, the bani suggests, starts with the head a little lower than before.

how: Sikhs who read Sukhmani Sahib begin with this salok of four bows, and Sikhs bow before the Guru Granth Sahib when they come into its presence.

o: I bow, a word of homage and salute
the Name, remembered at the start of prayer
I ask, a word that opens a request

games.q: the four bows — tap the pairs.
p: the primal Guru, of the beginning
the Guru through all the ages

s: Sukhmani opens with a teaching about peace
it opens with four bows to the Guru.
it closes each of the salok's four lines.
in this salok, the Guru bowed to is the One beyond time
the beginning, every age, truth itself.

games.q: you're about to begin a long bani about peace. how does Guru Arjan start Sukhmani?
o: with a promise of peace for the reader.
with four bows to the Guru.
with a story about his own life.
games.why: aad gure namah, jugaad gure namah, satgure namah, sri gurdeve namah: four bows before a single teaching.

practice: Sit up comfortably, breathe in, and as you breathe out let your head lower slowly, chin toward your chest, as far as feels easy.
Stay a breath or two, noticing what it's like to be a little lower, then rise; repeat it four times if you like, one for each line. If you pray, whisper aad gure namah.
